1. The completed scheduled unital sampling theorem

Fix a rational bound $\rho_0$ on the grouped Hamiltonian strength divided by $\gamma$. Consider arbitrary rational piecewise-constant onsite and nearest-neighbour two-body Hamiltonians $H(t)$, with
$\sup_t\|H_e(t)\|\le h,
\qquad
h/\gamma\le \rho_0.$
Here all contributions on the same physical support are grouped before applying the bound. For an input specified instead by individual term bounds and fixed incidence, a corresponding grouped bound follows by summing those bounds.

Take uniform replacement noise, so that $\eta_z=0$, any supplied rational product input, and any supplied finite rational one-site POVMs. Write $\tau=\gamma T$. Under the same sufficient condition as the designated Dots theorem,
$r_8(\tau)=307584+\lceil60\rho_0\tau\rceil,
\qquad
\tau\ge76932+2\lceil\log_2r_8(\tau)\rceil,$
the entire joint output law admits a classical sampler with unconditional TV error at most $\epsilon$ and worst-case bit work
$\boxed{
\operatorname{poly}_{\mathrm{class}}(B)
\left(\frac{nB}{\epsilon}\right)^{C_{\mathrm{class}}}.
}$
The exponent is a finite computable class constant. It does not grow with the supplied schedule length or time. Every schedule segment, rational entry, endpoint, POVM effect and outcome label is included in $B$.

Arbitrarily large binary times use the unital mixing shortcut. They are not simulated for their numerical duration. The requested time is never increased to make it qualify.

This is a full sampling theorem within its stated sector. Its restrictions remain substantive:


- the perturbation strength is zero;
- strong interactions are onsite or nearest-neighbour two-body;
- the sufficient qualifying-time condition, or an independently applicable mixing shortcut, must hold.

It therefore does not establish the requested positive nonunital neighbourhood or cover every early transient.
